title: Ἰκτῖνος χρεμετίζων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 136. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A kite had a voice unlike others, a shrill one.
sentences.n: ἄλλην here is 'other than the rest', the cry that belongs to the kite and to no other bird. The phrase is compressed and its exact force is not certain; the fable settles the sense, since everything in it turns on the bird's own voice against a borrowed one.

sentences.t: Ἵππου δὲ ἀκούσας καλῶς χρεμετίζοντος, μιμούμενος τὸν ἵππον καὶ συνεχῶς τοῦτο ποιῶν καὶ ταύτην μὴ καλῶς ἐκμαθών, καὶ τῆς ἰδίας φωνῆς ἐστέρηται, καὶ οὔτε τὴν τοῦ ἵππου ἔσχεν οὔτε τὴν πρώτην.
sentences.tr: Hippou de akousas kalōs chremetizontos, mimoumenos ton hippon kai synechōs touto poiōn kai tautēn mē kalōs ekmathōn, kai tēs idias phōnēs esterētai, kai oute tēn tou hippou eschen oute tēn prōtēn.
sentences.l: But having heard a horse neighing finely, imitating the horse and doing this continually and not having learned that voice well, he has both been robbed of his own voice and got neither the horse's nor his first one.
sentences.i: But when he heard a horse neigh finely, he set to imitating the horse, and kept at it without ever learning that voice well; and so he has been robbed of the voice that was his own, and has neither the horse's nor his first.
sentences.n: ἀκούω takes the genitive of what is heard, and the participle χρεμετίζοντος agrees with it: one hears the horse in the act of neighing. Four participles carry the whole story and only two finite verbs close it — the ordinary shape of a fable's narrative. The two καί before the finite verbs are correlative, 'both … and'. ἐστέρηται is a perfect: the loss is not an event but a standing condition.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ εὐτελεῖς καὶ φθονεροὶ ζηλοῦντες τοῦ παρὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν φύσιν καὶ τῶν κατὰ φύσιν στεροῦνται.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi euteleis kai phthoneroi zēlountes tou para tēn heautōn physin kai tōn kata physin sterountai.
sentences.l: That the mean and the envious, striving after what is beyond their own nature, are robbed even of what is according to nature.
sentences.i: The story shows that mean and envious men, straining after what lies beyond their own nature, lose even what nature gave them.
sentences.n: The introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ζηλοῦντες governs the genitive τοῦ παρὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν φύσιν: ζηλόω can name in the genitive the thing coveted or emulated. στεροῦνται then takes its own genitive, τῶν κατὰ φύσιν, of what is lost, with καί before it meaning 'even'. εὐτελής is 'of small cost' and so 'of no account'.
